Introdução: A Necessidade de Mudança de Abordagem Contexto Operacional As forças de segurança e militares ao redor do mundo enfrentam um desafio crescente: a necessidade de intervir em situações complexas sem recorrer à força letal desnecessária. Tradicionalmente, a abordagem baseada puramente em táticas militares ou policiais convencionais tem resultadod em elevadas taxas de casualties entre civis, erosão da confiança das comunidades e, em muitos casos, consolidação do poder dos grupos criminosos que se fintem operadores legítimos. 1.1 A Falha dos Modelos Tradicionais O modelo tradicional de "identificar, perseguir, neutralizar" esbarra em limitações crucuais: Falha na Distinção: Não consegue diferenciar entre combatentes reais, cúmplices menores e civis envolvidos por circunstância; Erosão da Legitimidade: Quando a população sente que é alvo de operações militarizadas, coopera menos com as forças de segurança; Radicalização Secundária: Operadores desnecessários podem criar mais reclutas do que neutralizam; Questões Jurídicas: Ações desproporcionais violam o Direito Internacional Humanitário e convenções de direitos humanos. Alerta Operacional Desempenhar ações com a mesma lógica que os grupos criminosos — mesmo que com intenções distintas — não apenas é antiético como compromete a legitimidade institucional. Crime é Crime, independentemente de quem o comete. 2. Diferenciação: Inocentes vs. Culpados Este é o conceito fundamental que separa operações eficazes das que perpetuam violência cíclica. Não existe "colateral" quando se falha na diferenciação. 2.1 Arquitetura de Participação Todo grupo criminoso ou de perturbação possui uma estrutura hierárquica que pode ser mapeada: 👑 Nível 1: Líderes Estratégicos Tomam decisões de longo prazo, organizam logistics, estabelecem agendas políticas ou criminais. Este grupo é o principal alvo para desmantelamento. 🎯 Nível 2: Executores Diretos Realizam ações específicas sob ordens. Podem ser persuadidos a deserir ou cooperar com informações sobre os líderes. 🛡️ Nível 3: Cúmplices por Circunstância Fornecedores locais, informadores não conscientes, comunidade que tolera por medo ou necesidade económica. 🌱 Nível 4: Potenciais Recrutas Jovens ou marginalizados susceptíveis a serem recrutados. Intervenção precoce aqui previne expansão do grupo. 2.2 Indicadores de Distinção Matriz de Análise de Participação Indicador Participação Ativa Participação Passiva Nenhuma Participação Conhecimento Operacional Conhece planos, locais, rotas Sabe que algo ocorre, mas não detalhes Ignora totalmente Contribuição Económica Financia, fornece recursos diretamente Compra produtos de forma incidental Não interage com economia do grupo Apoio Logístico Hospeda, transporta intencionalmente Não oferece resistência, mas não ajuda Coopera com autoridades Motivação Ideologia, ganância, vingança ativa Medo, necessidade económica Neutralidade ou oposição Princípio Operacional Antes de qualquer intervenção, a questão fundamental deve ser: "Esta pessoa é essencial para a estrutura do grupo, ou é um elo que pode ser substituído sem comprometer as operações?" Research verified 2025-2026 Handbook flow. 0 — Introduction: What Gentoo Is (And Is Not) Welcome, new friend. If you know nothing about Gentoo , start here. Gentoo is a source-based Linux distribution. Most distributions give you prebuilt binaries. Gentoo gives you recipes called ebuilds and a package manager called Portage with its famous command emerge . You compile software for your machine with your flags. Result: total control, total learning, total responsibility. This means install takes hours, sometimes days. Tip: this is normal. Gentoo is a teacher that charges tuition in compile time. You will choose init system ( OpenRC default classic, or systemd ), USE flags (global options like -gnome -kde pulseaudio ), profile , kernel type, bootloader, filesystem. Nothing hidden. Who should install Gentoo ? Curious people who want to understand Linux from disk label to desktop pixel. Who should not? Anyone needing a 20 -minute install before a meeting. Tip: keep a second computer or phone nearby for docs and coffee. Official sources you will use constantly: Handbook:AMD64 overview, Full Installation guide, Gentoo Wiki , forums.gentoo.org , packages.gentoo.org , bugs.gentoo.org . Bookmark them now. Tip: never follow random blog commands blindly; always cross-check the Handbook version for your arch. Versions in this guide: arch amd64 , UEFI + GPT assumed, OpenRC default with systemd notes. What you need: 64 -bit PC, 4 GB RAM minimum ( 8 GB+ happy), 40 GB disk minimum ( 100 GB+ for desktop + sources), wired net preferred, 8 GB USB stick, backup of all data. Tip: wired Ethernet saves hours of Wi-Fi firmware pain on first install. Time: 1 evening for base, 1-2 days for desktop + kernel + hardening. Security mindset from zero: we will verify downloads, encrypt where sensible, harden kernel, use SELinux or AppArmor options, firewall with nftables , least privilege, updates. Tip: security is a process, not a package. Every step below has a security note. 1 — Boot Media, Networking, Disks Step 1 : get media from gentoo.org/downloads/amd64 . Two flavors: Minimal Installation CD (small, text only) and LiveGUI (graphical). Tip: newbies take LiveGUI for comfort, Minimal for focus. Both boot same Handbook path. Verify checksum/signature per Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Media . Write with balenaEtcher , Rufus , Ventoy , or dd . Example: dd if= install-amd64-minimal.iso of= /dev/sdX bs= 4M status=progress. Tip: triple-check /dev/sdX with lsblk or you wipe the wrong disk. Boot in UEFI mode if target is UEFI. Connect net: NetworkManager on LiveGUI, or net-setup / ip + wpa_supplicant on Minimal. Test with ping 8.8.8.8 and ping gentoo.org . Tip: if Wi-Fi needs firmware, plug cable now; fight Wi-Fi after install. Set sshd password if you want remote help, and set clock with chrony / ntpd . Step 2 — disks: see Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Disks . Use lsblk , fdisk -l , gdisk or parted . We assume UEFI + GPT. Layout: 1 GiB EFI System Partition FAT32, swap (match RAM if hibernate, else 4-8 GB ), rest for root ext4 or btrfs or xfs + optional /home . Tip: separate /home saves future reinstall pain. LUKS-encrypt root/home now if laptop — see Security chapter. Example with parted : mklabel gpt, mkpart ESP fat32 1MiB 1025MiB , set 1 esp on, mkpart swap 1025MiB 9GiB , mkpart root 9GiB 100% . Format: mkfs.fat -F32 /dev/nvme0n1p1 , mkswap + swapon , mkfs.ext4 or mkfs.btrfs -L gentoo . Mount root at /mnt/gentoo , mkdir /mnt/gentoo/efi and mount ESP there (Handbook UEFI path) or /boot for BIOS layout. Tip: mount ESP at /efi for systemd-boot/dist-kernel style, at /boot/efi only if you know why. Sources: Handbook Media, Handbook Disks, Arch Wiki EFI/GPT pages for background, Gentoo Wiki LUKS articles. Tip: photograph partition table with phone before formatting — future you says thanks. 2 — Stage3, Chroot, Portage Basics Step 3 — stage: a stage 3 is your seed system, separate from ISO. Pick at gentoo.org/downloads/amd64 matching init: stage3-amd64-openrc or stage3-amd64-systemd , multilib default, desktop flavor if graphical (name contains desktop). See Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Stage . Tip: desktop stage saves hours of USE-flag wrestling for GNOME/KDE. Download + .DIGESTS + .asc, verify with sha512sum and gpg . Unpack with tar xpvf stage3-*.tar.xz --xattrs-include='*.*' --numeric-owner inside /mnt/gentoo . Tip: --numeric-owner and xattrs are not optional; skipping breaks permissions. Step 4 — chroot: copy DNS: cp --dereference /etc/resolv.conf /mnt/gentoo/etc/ . Mount proc sys dev run or use arch-chroot /mnt/gentoo helper. For UEFI mount ESP at /efi before chroot. See Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Base . Inside: emerge-webrsync to fetch Portage tree snapshot, then optional emerge --sync . Read news with eselect news read . Tip: always read news before first big emerge; it warns about profile/migration breakage. Select profile: eselect profile list , eselect profile set N . Example desktop plasma or gnome , with systemd variant if needed. Check with eselect profile show . Configure make.conf : COMMON_FLAGS= -O2 -march=native -pipe , MAKEOPTS= -jN+1 where N =cores, USE flags, VIDEO_CARDS, INPUT_DEVICES, ACCEPT_LICENSE. Tip: -march=native is fast but binaries not portable; use generic x86-64 if you clone disks. Set eselect repository , mirrors with mirrorselect . Configure system files: /etc/fstab (use UUIDs from blkid ), hostname in /etc/conf.d/hostname ( OpenRC ) or /etc/hostname ( systemd ), timezone via eselect timezone / symlink /etc/localtime , locale in /etc/locale.gen + locale-gen + eselect locale , keymap, root password with passwd , networking ( NetworkManager easiest for desktop, dhcpcd / netifrc for servers). Tip: UUID in fstab prevents boot fail after disk reorder. Sources: Handbook Stage, Handbook Base, Wiki: Portage/Profiles , Wiki: MAKEOPTS , man make.conf , man emerge . Tip: keep a text log of every command; Gentoo forums love logs when helping. 3 — Kernel: Distribution vs Manual Compile See Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Kernel . Three roads: sys-kernel/gentoo-kernel-bin (prebuilt, fastest, great for newbies), sys-kernel/gentoo-kernel (source-built distro kernel, auto updates, needs installkernel + initramfs), sys-kernel/gentoo-sources (fully manual, you configure/compile). Tip: start with -bin to get to desktop today, switch to manual later for learning. Distro kernel path: emerge --ask sys-kernel/gentoo-kernel-bin sys-kernel/installkernel sys-kernel/dracut sys-firmware/linux-firmware sof-firmware sys-firmware/intel-microcode amd-ucode . Dracut builds initramfs for LUKS/LVM/btrfs. Check /efi or /boot for vmlinuz-6.x + initramfs . Tip: install linux-firmware + microcode before first boot or Wi-Fi/GPU may vanish. Enable installkernel USE for grub or systemd-boot layout. Manual path: emerge --ask sys-kernel/gentoo-sources sys-apps/pciutils usbutils , cd /usr/src/linux , make menuconfig (needs ncurses ). Essentials: 64 -bit, EFI stub, NVMe, SATA AHCI, ext4/btrfs built-in not module if root, drm amdgpu/i915/nouveau , sound, USB, networking. Tip: run lspci -k and lsmod on LiveGUI, photo it, enable exactly that hardware first. Build: make -j$(nproc) , make modules_install install . Takes 20 min to 2 hours by CPU. Keep .config backup in /root/kernel-config-YYYY-MM-DD . Initramfs when needed (LUKS/LVM/btrfs/UEFI): dracut --hostonly --kver 6.x.y-gentoo or genkernel --install initramfs . Verify ls -lh /boot /efi . Tip: if root is LUKS, test cryptsetup open before reboot or you lock yourself out. Sources: Handbook Kernel, Wiki: Kernel/Gentoo Kernel Upgrade Guide , Wiki: Dracut , Wiki: Genkernel , kernel.org docs. Tip: keep one known-good kernel + one new; never delete all old kernels. 4 — Bootloader, First Reboot, Post-Install Base See Handbook:AMD64/Installation/Bootloader . Default sys-boot/grub handles BIOS+UEFI. UEFI alt sys-boot/systemd-boot (simple, fast). Install: emerge --ask sys-boot/grub efibootmgr os-prober (skip os-prober if single boot). grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/efi --bootloader-id=Gentoo , then grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg . Tip: --efi-directory must match where you mounted ESP (/efi vs /boot); mismatch = unbootable. For systemd-boot : bootctl install --esp-path=/efi , loader entries in /efi/loader/entries/gentoo.conf pointing to vmlinuz + initramfs + root UUID + rw . Tip: systemd-boot needs manual entry update per kernel unless installkernel hooks do it — check after each upgrade. Exit chroot, unmount: exit , umount -l /mnt/gentoo/dev{/shm,/pts,} , umount -R /mnt/gentoo , reboot , remove USB. First boot: login root, check dmesg | grep -i -E 'error|firmware|fail' , ip a , ping . Add user: useradd -m -G wheel,audio,video,usb,portage -s /bin/bash alice , passwd alice , install sudo + visudo (uncomment wheel). Tip: never daily-drive as root; sudo + wheel from day one. Base update discipline: emerge --sync (or emaint sync -a ), emerge --ask --verbose --update --deep --newuse @world , emerge --depclean , revdep-rebuild , eclean-dist --deep . Tip: update weekly, read elog with eselect news + elogv; small frequent merges beat yearly breakage. Sources: Handbook Bootloader, Wiki: GRUB2 , Wiki: Systemd-boot , man sudoers . Tip: snapshot btrfs subvolume or Clonezilla image right after first good boot. 5 — Kernel Hardening, MAC, Toolchain Security Hardening is where Gentoo shines. Baseline: updated kernel ( 6.x stable, never ancient), least modules, Secure Boot with custom keys via sbctl or sbsigntools if threat model needs. Tip: enable Secure Boot only after normal boot works; debug one layer at a time. Kernel self-protection (manual or via gentoo-kernel + sysctl): enable STACKPROTECTOR_STRONG , STRICT_KERNEL_RWX , STRICT_MODULE_RWX , SLAB_FREELIST_HARDENED , SHUFFLE_PAGE_ALLOCATOR , RANDOMIZE_BASE (KASLR), HARDENED_USERCOPY , SECURITY_LOCKDOWN_LSM , PAGE_TABLE_ISOLATION , RETPOLINE / IBRS mitigations, DEBUG_WX to find WX, disable /dev/mem /dev/kmem , LDISC_AUTOLOAD off, USER_NS_UNPRIVILEGED restrict if not needing containers. Tip: copy hardened .config fragment to /root and diff after each make olddefconfig. See Wiki: Hardened Gentoo , gentoo-hardened overlay, KSPP checklists. Mandatory Access Control — pick one : SELinux (strongest, steepest; selinux-base-policy , relabel, setenforce 1 ) or AppArmor (easier, profiles via apparmor-utils , aa-enforce ) . Tip: newbies start with AppArmor + firewall; graduate to SELinux on second install. Add hardened malloc via sys-libs/mimalloc-hw or hardened_malloc overlay for browsers, firejail or bubblewrap sandbox for Firefox . Toolchain: gcc with -fstack-protector-strong -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -Wl,-z,RelRO,-z,Now -fPIE -pie via CFLAGS / LDFLAGS or hardened profile ( eselect profile hardened). Enable PIE + RELRO + NOW + SSP , verify with hardening-check / checksec . Tip: hardened flags can break exotic packages; keep per-package exceptions in /etc/portage/env, not global weaken. Boot/filesystem: LUKS2 ( cryptsetup ) with argon2id , detached header backup offline, fscrypt or eCryptfs only if needed, auditd rules for /etc/passwd /etc/shadow /boot , AIDE or samhain integrity DB on read-only USB. Tip: print LUKS recovery key on paper, store offsite; digital-only backup dies with disk. Sources: Gentoo Hardened project, Wiki: SELinux , Wiki: AppArmor , KSPP (kernel self-protection), man cryptsetup . Tip: change one hardening knob per reboot so you know what broke boot. 6 — Desktop: Plasma / GNOME, Graphics, Sound Pick profile first: eselect profile list | grep desktop , set default/linux/amd64/23.0/desktop/plasma or .../desktop/gnome (+ systemd variant if on systemd ). Set VIDEO_CARDS= amdgpu radeon intel nvidia as needed, INPUT_DEVICES= libinput synaptics . Tip: wrong VIDEO_CARDS = black screen; lspci | grep -i vga first. X or Wayland: xorg-server + xinit for classic, or Wayland via plasma-meta / gnome sessions. Install: emerge --ask kde-plasma/plasma-meta kde-apps/kdecore-meta sddm for KDE Plasma , or emerge --ask gnome-base/gnome gdm for GNOME . Lighter: i3 , sway , Xfce via xfce4-meta . Enable DM: rc-update add sddm default ( OpenRC ) or systemctl enable sddm ( systemd ). Tip: test with startx as user before enabling DM; DM hides errors. Firmware + microcode + graphics: linux-firmware amdgpu-ucode intel-microcode amd-ucode mesa vulkan-loader libva-vdpau-driver , kernel DRM built-in. Sound: pipewire wireplumber pipewire-pulse alsa-utils pavucontrol . Tip: PipeWire + WirePlumber is modern default; enable pipewire service per user. Fonts: noto , corefonts , fontconfig . Printing: cups . Bluetooth: bluez . Apps baseline: firefox (set USE=hardened pie ), thunderbird , libreoffice , vlc , gimp , keepassxc , flatpak optional for closed apps. Tip: Flatpak for Spotify/Discord/Steam keeps base clean; native emerge for everything else. Sources: Wiki: KDE , Wiki: GNOME , Wiki: Xorg , Wiki: PipeWire , eselect profile docs. Tip: emerge -pv before big desktop merge to see USE changes; veto surprises early. 7 — Network, Firewall, SSH, Updates, Backups Firewall default-deny with nftables (modern) or iptables legacy. Install nftables , enable, rules: allow lo , established, 22 only from LAN if needed, 80/443 out, drop rest, rate-limit SSH 3/min . Or use ufw / firewalld wrapper. Tip: test firewall over console first; lockout over SSH with no IPMI is a long walk. Add fail2ban for SSH, usbguard for BadUSB. SSH: openssh , PermitRootLogin no , PasswordAuthentication no (keys in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys 600 ), Port 2222 optional, AllowUsers alice . Tip: ssh-copy-id then disable passwords; one key leak beats thousand brute forces. VPN: wireguard-tools for road warriors. DNS: systemd-resolved or dnscrypt-proxy + DNSSEC. Updates + integrity: weekly emaint sync -a; emerge -uDN @world; emerge --depclean; revdep-rebuild; eclean-dist -d; updatedb; aide --check . Enable elogv / eselect news . Backups: borgbackup or restic to external LUKS disk + offsite, test restore quarterly. Tip: untested backup is rumor. Restore one file now to prove it works. Browser + user hardening: Firefox with uBlock Origin , NoScript or uMatrix , KeepassXC , separate profiles, bubblewrap / flatpak sandbox. Tip: Wayland + PipeWire + Flatpak Firefox is safest easy desktop sandbox. Sources: Wiki: Nftables , Wiki: OpenSSH , Wiki: WireGuard , Gentoo Security Handbook . Tip: run lynis audit or tiger check quarterly; fix reds first. 8 — Extra Security, Tips, Troubleshooting, Next Steps Extra: securelevel via sysctl kernel.kexec_load_disabled=1 kernel.dmesg_restrict=1 kernel.kptr_restrict=2 kernel.perf_event_paranoid=2 kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled=2 net.core.bpf_jit_harden=2 vm.mmap_rnd_bits=32 in /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf . sys-kernel/linux-firmware minimal (strip unused). Disable Bluetooth / Thunderbolt in BIOS if unused. Tip: sysctl + reboot + sysctl -a | grep setting to confirm; typos silently fail. Physical: BIOS password, boot order lock, LUKS + TPM2 + PIN via clevis optional, screen lock 5 min, usbguard block new devices when locked. Tip: encrypt swap or disable hibernate; cleartext swap leaks keys. Supply chain: verify ISOs, use gpg , app-portage/gemato , avoid random overlays; add eselect repository overlays sparingly. Troubleshooting: no boot? Check ESP mount, grub.cfg UUIDs, dracut --regenerate-all . Black screen? VIDEO_CARDS + firmware + eselect opengl . No net? dhcpcd vs NetworkManager conflict — pick one . Merge fail? Read build.log, emerge --info , search bugs.gentoo.org + forums with exact error. Tip: pastebin emerge --info + build log when asking help; helpers ignore vague 'it broke'. Next: join forums , IRC #gentoo , Reddit r/Gentoo , read GWN weekly news. Try distcc / ccache for speed, binpkg host for laptops. Tip: ccache size 10-20 GB cuts recompiles massively on desktop. Master source list: Handbook AMD64 + Full, Installation Media/Disks/Stage/Base/Kernel/Bootloader, Portage Profiles, KDE/GNOME/PipeWire/Nftables/OpenSSH/WireGuard/SELinux/AppArmor/Hardened Wiki pages, man pages for emerge make.conf fstab cryptsetup gpg sudoers sysctl . Tip: keep this HTML offline on USB; best rescue disk is docs you own. Gentoo installed? Harden weekly: emaint , emerge , eclean , aide , borgbackup . Tip: you now own your system — keep notes, keep backups, keep curiosity. Good luck from 0 to root.

Porque é preciso testar o código, e o teste é como se sabe que o código funciona, mesmo que se possa rever o código para entender como o «problema» foi resolvido e para ver se há algumas linhas extra que não precisam de existir naquele pedaço de código em particular. kernelDisks: Home Kernel / Storage Kconfig Kconfig · disks, partitions, LVM, FAT32, NTFS Kernel disks: bring the disk up before anything else The storage stack is the one place where "make it a module" is answered by a single question: does the kernel need it before it can load modules? This page walks the storage menu from the block layer down to the filesystems — disk drivers, MSDOS_PARTITION and EFI_PARTITION , device mapper and LVM, FAT32 for the ESP, and both NTFS drivers — so each letter is a decision with a reason. <*> vs <M> GPT / MBR device mapper + LVM vfat + ntfs3 01 The one rule that decides the letter Networking can wait until userspace runs. Storage cannot: the kernel has to read the disk to find /sbin/init , and it has to read it with code that is already in memory . Whatever sits between the disk and the root mount is therefore a candidate for =y , and everything else is a cheap module you can unload. Marker Type Meaning <*> tristate, y Inside the kernel image; available before any module is loaded <M> tristate, m A .ko file; loadable, unloadable, and absent if /lib/modules is wrong < > tristate, n Not compiled at all — the code does not exist on this machine [*] boolean On or off; there is no module form, so the choice is real and permanent {M} forced Selected by another option; you cannot make it =y unless the parent is =y The practical test Ask: is this needed to mount the root filesystem, or to mount a filesystem that a boot service mounts before userspace can rescue the machine? If yes and there is no initramfs on the box — an appliance, a vendor image, a kernel you boot directly with -append root=/dev/nvme0n1p2 — then build it in. If no, a module costs one modprobe and saves memory on every machine that never touches it. The initramfs changes the arithmetic, and that is why most distributions ship all of this as modules: the initramfs carries sd_mod , dm-crypt , lvm and ext4 , loads them, and only then switches root. Build in what the image would need if the initramfs were broken or absent — which is exactly the failure mode you will meet at 3 a.m. 02 Where the truth lives Symbol names move between releases and the menu grouping is opinion, not documentation. The kernel tree defines every symbol; the running kernel can tell you what it was built with. # what this kernel says about itself uname -r zcat /proc/config.gz | grep -E "CONFIG_(EFI_PARTITION|BLK_DEV_DM|DM_CRYPT|VFAT_FS|NTFS3_FS)=" ls /boot/config-"$(uname -r)" 2>/dev/null # the authoritative definitions grep -n "config EFI_PARTITION" -A 10 block/partitions/Kconfig grep -rn "config NTFS3_FS" -A 14 fs/ntfs3/Kconfig grep -n "config FAT_DEFAULT_IOCHARSET" -A 8 fs/fat/Kconfig # change without menuconfig, then see exactly what moved cp .config .config.old scripts/config --file .config --enable EFI_PARTITION scripts/config --file .config --module VFAT_FS scripts/config --file .config --enable DM_INIT make olddefconfig scripts/diffconfig .config.old .config scripts/config --state CONFIG_X prints the current value without changing it, which is the quickest way to audit a vendor config before you trust it. And /proc/filesystems lists what the running kernel can actually mount — a name missing there is not a mount option problem. 03 The chain to the root filesystem Read it bottom-up: the bus driver finds the disk, the block layer exposes it, the partition parser splits it, the mapper (if any) reassembles it, and the filesystem driver reads it. Any missing link produces a VFS: Cannot open root device and a rescue prompt, with no clue about which link broke. Link Symbol Why built-in without an initramfs Block layer BLOCK [*] Everything below is inside it; it is not optional Disk driver BLK_DEV_SD , BLK_DEV_NVME , VIRTIO_BLK The root disk is not visible at all until this loads Partition table EFI_PARTITION , MSDOS_PARTITION The disk appears, but no p1 / p2 nodes exist Mapper BLK_DEV_DM , DM_CRYPT , LVM targets Root on LUKS or on an LV is unreachable without it Filesystem EXT4_FS , XFS_FS , BTRFS_FS VFS: Cannot open root device even though it is there Two links that fail quietly A missing partition parser is worse than a missing driver, because the disk still shows up: you get /dev/nvme0n1 , no partitions, and a filesystem signature nobody can mount. A missing filesystem looks like "root device not found" too, even though lsblk is perfectly happy. Both are one grep away in /proc/config.gz . 04 Disk drivers: SD, NVMe, virtio # SCSI/ATA low level CONFIG_BLK_DEV_SD=y # sd_mod: the sdX names, ATA and USB UAS disk CONFIG_ATA=y CONFIG_SATA_AHCI=y CONFIG_ATA_PIIX=y # IDE-emulated mode in older QEMU CONFIG_SCSI=y CONFIG_SCSI_VIRTIO=y # virtio-scsi controller # NVMe CONFIG_BLK_DEV_NVME=y # the whole nvme stack; no sdX alias # virtual and removable CONFIG_VIRTIO_BLK=y CONFIG_MMC_BLOCK=m # SD cards and eMMC CONFIG_MMC_SDHCI=m CONFIG_USB_STORAGE=m CONFIG_BLK_DEV_SR=m # optical / srX, needed to read install media CONFIG_UAS=m # USB Attached SCSI, much faster than usb-storage Note that BLK_DEV_SD is not "the SATA driver": it is the SCSI disk class driver, and every SATA disk in AHCI mode, every USB mass-storage device and every virtio-scsi disk goes through it. A kernel with SATA_AHCI but without BLK_DEV_SD finds the controller and shows no disk at all — the most common "my build does not see the disk" answer. NVMe is different: BLK_DEV_NVME registers its own block device, so there is no dependency on sd_mod . On a machine that boots from NVMe with no initramfs, this one symbol must be =y , and it is worth building in even with an initramfs, because the initramfs is written from the module list of the machine that generated it. 05 Partitions — and the one everybody forgets CONFIG_PARTITION_ADVANCED=y # [*] the gate for everything below CONFIG_EFI_PARTITION=y # GPT — modern disks, and the reason pN vanished CONFIG_MSDOS_PARTITION=y # MBR — USB sticks, old VMs, hybrid images CONFIG_OF_PARTITION=y # devicetree partitions, ARM boards CONFIG_BSD_DISKLABEL=m CONFIG_SOLARIS_X86_PARTITION=m CONFIG_UNIXWARE_DISKLABEL=m Symbol Form Symptom when missing EFI_PARTITION bool [*] GPT disk shows as one device; lsblk lists no children MSDOS_PARTITION bool [*] MBR USB stick mounts only as a whole disk PARTITION_ADVANCED bool [*] The exotic parsers are not even offered in the menu BLK_DEV_LOOP tristate mount -o loop image.iso fails; snap and AppImage break BLK_DEV_NBD tristate Network block devices unavailable BLK_DEV_RAM tristate No /dev/ram0 ; some rescue tooling assumes it These are booleans, so "make GPT a module" is not on the table: either the kernel understands GPT or it does not. Build both parsers in. MSDOS_PARTITION costs a few kilobytes and is the difference between a rescue stick that mounts and one that does not. Hybrid and 4K-sector disks A hybrid MBR/GPT image needs both parsers, and a 4Kn disk needs nothing extra in the config — but a partition table written for 512-byte sectors on a 4K-native disk will be rejected, and the message is about the partition table, not about Kconfig. Check with blockdev --getss /dev/sdX . 06 Block layer extras worth building Symbol Recommended What it buys BLK_DEV_INITRD =y Initramfs support; without it no modern distro kernel boots BLK_DEV_BSG =m sg3_utils , smartctl , SCSI generic access BLK_CGROUP =y I/O limits per container and per systemd slice IOSCHED_BFQ =m Desktop fairness; the scheduler itself is optional MQ_IOSCHED_KYBER =m Low-latency reads on NVMe BLK_DEV_THROTTLING =y Per-cgroup IOPS and bandwidth caps BLK_DEV_INTEGRITY =y if T10-PI End-to-end data integrity on enterprise disks BLK_DEV_WRITE_MOUNTED =n Refuses writes to a mounted block device — a real footgun closed BLK_DEV_WRITE_MOUNTED is recent and worth knowing: with it enabled (the historical default) root can still dd over a mounted filesystem and corrupt it. Disabling it turns a silent disaster into an EBUSY , which is the kind of change a kernel config makes better than any warning banner. 07 Device mapper and LVM The first correction: there is no CONFIG_LVM . LVM is a userspace tool ( lvm2 ) that drives the kernel's device-mapper targets; the kernel side is a handful of DM_* symbols. Searching a config for LVM and finding nothing is not a missing feature. CONFIG_MD=y CONFIG_BLK_DEV_DM=y # =y if root is on LVM/LUKS and there is no initramfs CONFIG_DM_INIT=y # [*] activate DM devices at boot, before the root mount CONFIG_DM_CRYPT=y # LUKS CONFIG_DM_SNAPSHOT=m # thin snapshots, backup windows CONFIG_DM_THIN_PROVISIONING=m # the modern LVM thin pool CONFIG_DM_CACHE=m # SSD cache in front of a slow LV CONFIG_DM_MIRROR=m CONFIG_DM_RAID=m CONFIG_DM_VERITY=m # read-only verified root images CONFIG_DM_INTEGRITY=m CONFIG_DM_MULTIPATH=m # two paths to the same SAN LUN CONFIG_DM_ZERO=m # sparse test devices # md/RAID is a different subsystem, do not confuse it with DM RAID CONFIG_MD_RAID0=m CONFIG_MD_RAID1=m CONFIG_MD_RAID456=m Symbol Form Missing it means BLK_DEV_DM tristate dmsetup cannot open /dev/mapper/control ; no LVM at all DM_INIT bool [*] Root on an LV needs an initramfs; without one, boot hangs at the root prompt DM_CRYPT tristate crypt: unknown target type ; LUKS unlock impossible DM_THIN_PROVISIONING tristate lvcreate --thin fails; the thin pool target is unknown DM_CACHE , DM_RAID tristate Only that LV type refuses to activate; the rest of LVM works MD_RAID456 tristate mdadm assembles nothing for RAID5/6 Build BLK_DEV_DM , DM_CRYPT and the thin target in when the root volume lives on them and the machine has no initramfs. Otherwise they are modules and the initramfs loads them — that is what update-initramfs is for, and why a kernel upgrade with a broken initramfs is a separate failure from a bad config. 08 LUKS and the crypto that must exist first DM_CRYPT=y is only half of an encrypted root. The cipher the volume was created with must be available at unlock time, and the defaults are not free: aes-xts-plain64 needs AES and XTS, and the key derivation needs a hash. CONFIG_DM_CRYPT=y CONFIG_CRYPTO_AES=y CONFIG_CRYPTO_XTS=y CONFIG_CRYPTO_SHA256=y CONFIG_CRYPTO_USER_API_SKCIPHER=m # only if userspace asks for ciphers by name CONFIG_KEYS=y CONFIG_ENCRYPTED_KEYS=y # systemd asks for a TPM-bound key CONFIG_BLK_INLINE_ENCRYPTION=m # eMMC/UFS hardware encryption The failure that looks like a wrong password cryptsetup: device-mapper: reload ioctl on … failed: Invalid argument during unlock is usually not a password problem: it is the cipher or hash module missing from the initramfs. Check /proc/crypto for xts(aes) before deciding the disk is lost. File-level encryption is a different stack: FS_ENCRYPTION (fscrypt) encrypts directories inside ext4 and F2FS and needs no device mapper at all, while DM_VERITY gives a read-only root whose blocks are hash-verified — the usual basis of an immutable appliance image. 09 FAT32: the format that boots machines FAT is not a legacy detail you can drop. The EFI system partition is FAT, most boot media is FAT, and camera cards, dashcams and firmware updaters are FAT. Three symbols do the work, and a fourth decides which characters survive the trip. CONFIG_FAT_FS=y # the core; vfat and msdos depend on it CONFIG_VFAT_FS=y # long names, the usual "vfat" — and the ESP CONFIG_MSDOS_FS=m # 8.3 names, FAT12/16; usually not needed CONFIG_EXFAT_FS=m # large cards, a different driver entirely # the charset housekeeping people skip CONFIG_NLS_CODEPAGE_437=y CONFIG_NLS_ISO8859_1=y CONFIG_NLS_UTF8=y CONFIG_FAT_DEFAULT_CODEPAGE=437 CONFIG_FAT_DEFAULT_IOCHARSET="utf8" Symbol Form Missing it means FAT_FS tristate unknown filesystem type 'vfat' ; fat is not even in /proc/filesystems VFAT_FS tristate The mount type named vfat does not exist — the common case MSDOS_FS tristate Only mount -t msdos fails; vfat still mounts the same disk NLS_UTF8 tristate, no prompt FAT-fs: IO charset utf8 not found , then unreadable names NLS_CODEPAGE_437 tristate Default codepage unavailable; the mount falls back or fails EXFAT_FS tristate Big SD cards need exfat / exfatprogs instead of vfat FAT_DEFAULT_IOCHARSET is a string, not a module, and it is the one setting that decides whether a Portuguese or Japanese filename appears intact. "utf8" is the right default for anything shared with another operating system; "iso8859-1" is the historic default and produces replacement characters on any name outside Latin-1. Is vfat boot-critical? Only on machines whose /boot is the ESP itself — some ARM boards, some unified-kernel images, and every setup that keeps kernels on the ESP. On ordinary x86 with a separate ext4 /boot , the firmware reads FAT and the kernel never does, so <M> is correct and expected. 10 NTFS: ntfs3 against the legacy driver Two kernel drivers carry the NTFS name and they are not the same thing. NTFS3_FS is the in-kernel read-write driver; NTFS_FS is the old read-mostly one that most people replaced years ago with the userspace FUSE driver ntfs-3g . Symbol What it is Recommended NTFS3_FS In-kernel driver, read-write, mount type ntfs3 <M> ; <*> only if mounted before modules load NTFS3_LZX_XPRESS Decompression for compressed NTFS files <M> when the volume uses compression NTFS_FS Legacy driver, mount type ntfs < > unless you have a reason NTFS_RW Limited write support for the legacy driver < > — it is the one that damages volumes NLS_UTF8 Charset for non-ASCII filenames <*> or <M> , same reasoning as FAT # the modern driver CONFIG_NTFS3_FS=m CONFIG_NTFS3_LZX_XPRESS=m # the legacy pair — leave both off # CONFIG_NTFS_FS is not set # CONFIG_NTFS_RW is not set # mount it, and check the driver that answered mount -t ntfs3 /dev/sdb1 /mnt/win findmnt -no FSTYPE,SOURCE /mnt/win What neither driver opens BitLocker volumes and disks in Intel RST / RAID mode are not NTFS volumes to the kernel: the encryption or the Intel metadata sits below the filesystem and no NTFS* symbol helps. Those need the volume unlocked in firmware first, which is a different page and a different failure. ntfs3 also handles the hibernated/fast-startup case badly: a Windows volume that was not shut down properly still looks dirty, and the driver will mount it read-only rather than risk a corrupted $LogFile . That is the intended behaviour, not a config problem — dmesg | grep ntfs3 says so in one line. 11 Filesystems you actually mount Symbol Recommended Where it appears EXT4_FS =y if root Almost every Debian and Ubuntu root; also /boot XFS_FS =m RHEL-family roots and large data volumes BTRFS_FS =m Snapshots, subvolumes, openSUSE/Fedora defaults F2FS_FS =m Flash-only devices, phones, some handhelds SQUASHFS =m Live images, snap packages, read-only overlays ISO9660_FS , UDF_FS =m CD/DVD and Blu-ray; UDF also covers large optical media TMPFS =y /dev/shm and /run ; systemd needs it early OVERLAY_FS =m Containers and live-system persistence FUSE_FS =m ntfs-3g, sshfs, rclone, and every userspace filesystem TMPFS is the odd one out in this table: it is not a disk filesystem, but a machine that cannot mount /run early does not reach a login prompt. Treat it like the console — always in. 12 Software that asks for the module A symbol name says nothing until you know which program calls it. The left column is the module, the middle is the software that fails without it, and the right is what that program is doing with it. If none of the software in a row is installed here, that module has no purpose on this machine. a VM snapshot needs the target present dm_snapshot lvm2 ( lvcreate -s ) Copy-on-write snapshots taken before an upgrade dm_multipath multipath-tools ( multipathd ) Two HBAs, one LUN; without it the second path becomes a second disk dm_verity veritysetup (cryptsetup package), systemd-veritysetup Hash-verified read-only images dm_integrity integritysetup Per-block checksums under a filesystem loop snapd , flatpak , AppImage, mount -o loop Mounts a file as if it were a disk; That is a config plan derived from the machine instead of from a blog, and it is the same list that tells you what to put in an initramfs. 13 Hardening by removing Every filesystem driver you build is code running with kernel privilege, parsing bytes from media an attacker may control — a USB stick in a parking lot is a delivered exploit. Removing the drivers removes the parser. # parsers worth deleting on a server that never uses them # CONFIG_HFS_FS is not set # CONFIG_HFSPLUS_FS is not set # CONFIG_JFS_FS is not set # CONFIG_UFS_FS is not set # CONFIG_GFS2_FS is not set # CONFIG_OCFS2_FS is not set # CONFIG_NILFS2_FS is not set # CONFIG_REISERFS_FS is not set # CONFIG_AFFS_FS is not set # and the block-level levers CONFIG_BLK_DEV_LOOP=m # needed by snap/flatpak, so module not built-in # CONFIG_BLK_DEV_NBD is not set # CONFIG_BLK_DEV_WRITE_MOUNTED is not set CONFIG_DEVMEM=n # already gone on most builds; /dev/mem is not a tool CONFIG_STRICT_DEVMEM=y Default mounts: noexec, nosuid and nodev on /tmp , /dev/shm and removable media costs nothing and blocks a whole class of tricks. Unloadable modules: MODULE_UNLOAD=n plus signed modules means an attacker cannot swap a driver, and you cannot replace one without a reboot. Verified root: DM_VERITY plus a read-only image turns "the disk changed" into a boot failure instead of a compromise. The cost is your rescue stick Removing vfat, exfat and NTFS means a machine that cannot read the USB stick you brought to repair it. kernelNetworking: Home Kernel / Networking Kconfig Kconfig · built-in vs module, symbol by symbol Kernel networking: what goes in, what gets loaded Every networking failure that begins with "operation not supported" is usually a symbol set to the wrong letter years earlier. This page explains the three markers in make menuconfig , gives the rule that decides built-in versus module, and then walks the networking menu option by option — routing tables, netfilter, bridges, tunnels, traffic control and eBPF — so the choice is a reason, not a reflex. <*> vs <M> policy routing netfilter + nftables tc / XDP 01 The markers, and what (*) really is The notation is the first thing tutorials blur. There is no (*) symbol in the kernel config; menuconfig draws three different markers, and confusing them is how people "enable routing" by ticking a boolean that only controls whether a module is even offered. You see Symbol type Means Can be unloaded? <*> tristate, value y Compiled into the kernel image No <M> tristate, value m Compiled as a separate .ko Yes, unless in use < > tristate, value n Not built at all — [*] boolean On or off only; there is no module form No {M} / {*} forced Selected by another option you enabled Only by disabling the parent That table answers half the question by itself: many routing features are booleans , so they show as [*] and cannot be modules at all. Where a symbol is a tristate, the decision is real. The rule that decides everything Build in what the machine needs before it can load modules ; make everything else a module. In practice: storage, console, the NIC the initramfs brings up, and anything the initramfs needs to reach the root filesystem. Networking beyond that is almost always a module — unless you intend to burn the bridge by disabling module loading. 02 Where the truth lives Never trust a blog for a symbol name — including this one. The kernel tree names its own symbols, and the running kernel can tell you what it was built with. # what am I running, and was this config even exposed? uname -r zcat /proc/config.gz | grep -E "CONFIG_(IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES|NF_CONNTRACK)=" ls /boot/config-"$(uname -r)" # the authoritative definition, in the source tree grep -n "config IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES" -A 12 net/ipv4/Kconfig scripts/config --file .config --state CONFIG_BRIDGE # change the config without menuconfig scripts/config --file .config --module BRIDGE make olddefconfig # resolve new symbols with defaults scripts/diffconfig .config.old .config # exactly what you changed localmodconfig is tempting — it keeps only the modules currently loaded. It is fine for a laptop, and a trap for a router: the modules your firewall needs may simply not be loaded on the build machine when you run it. 03 What must be built in Symbol Why it cannot be a module here VIRTIO_NET Cloud and VM images whose root disk is virtual need the NIC before root mounts E1000E , IGB , IXGBE The physical port used for PXE, NFS root or iSCSI boot BRIDGE Only if the root filesystem is behind a bridge (rare) or modules are disabled VLAN_8021Q When the management interface is tagged and configured in the initramfs BONDING When the boot interface is a bond PACKET If the machine's only diagnostic is tcpdump on a rescue image with no modules Everything else on this page is a module in a sane configuration. The price of =y is permanent memory and a permanently larger trusted computing base; the price of =m is a load step and the risk that the module is not there after a kernel upgrade. 04 Routing and policy routing # Networking support -> Networking options CONFIG_NET=y # [*] the whole stack CONFIG_INET=y # [*] TCP/IP CONFIG_IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER=y # [*] unlocks the routing extras below CONFIG_IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y # [*] ip rule, policy routing CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH=y # [*] several nexthops per route CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_CLASSID=y # [*] tc classification by route CONFIG_IPV6_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y # [*] the same for IPv6 CONFIG_IPV6_SUBTREES=y # [*] source-based IPv6 lookups Symbol Form Turn it on when IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER bool [*] Always on a router or firewall; it gates the rest IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES bool [*] You use ip rule , VRFs, or anything with multiple routing tables IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH bool [*] Two uplinks, or the ECMP lab from the GNS3 page IP_ROUTE_CLASSID bool [*] Traffic control keyed on a route class IPV6 tristate You have IPv6 — build in if the address is assigned before modules load These are booleans, so "make it a module" is not an option and the question becomes whether to enable them at all. A kernel without IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES still routes; it just ignores every second table, and ip rule commands appear to succeed while doing nothing. 05 Netfilter, conntrack, NAT # core: everything else depends on these CONFIG_NETFILTER=y CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK=m <M> the state table CONFIG_NF_NAT=m <M> NAT engine, needed by MASQUERADE CONFIG_NF_TABLES=m <M> the nftables core CONFIG_NF_TABLES_INET=m <M> one table for v4 and v6 CONFIG_NFT_CT=m <M> ct expression CONFIG_NETFILTER_XTABLES=m <M> the xtables compatibility layer CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_MASQUERADE=m CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK_FTP=m # helpers: load only what you need Symbol Form Effect if missing NF_CONNTRACK tristate No stateful rules, no NAT, no conntrack tool NF_NAT tristate MASQUERADE and DNAT simply do not exist NF_TABLES tristate nft reports no such file or unsupported NETFILTER_XTABLES tristate Legacy iptables rules fail to apply NF_CONNTRACK_FTP etc. tristate Only that protocol's helper is absent — good default Modules are fine here — until you disable modules Debian and every mainstream distro ship netfilter as modules, and it works. Build it in when you plan to set kernel.modules_disabled=1 after boot, or when the firewall must be able to drop packets before any userspace process has run. 06 Bridges, VLANs, bonds, virtual links Symbol Recommended Needed by BRIDGE <M> Anything that bridges: VMs, containers, the GNS3 switch BRIDGE_NETFILTER <M> iptables on bridged traffic; Docker needs it VLAN_8021Q <M> ip link add ... type vlan BONDING <M> LACP and failover bonds MACVLAN / IPVLAN <M> Many addresses on one NIC, container networking VETH <M> Namespaces, containers, test topologies DUMMY <M> A stable interface that stays up with no cable IFB <M> Ingress shaping — redirecting ingress into a qdisc TUN <M> VPNs and user-space tunnels; also creates tap These are cheap modules and there is no security reason to build them in. The one exception is a host that cannot load modules at all, where every link type the boot scripts create must be present in the image. 07 Tunnels and VPNs Symbol Recommended Note WIREGUARD <M> One module, no dependencies; "Unknown device type" means it is missing VXLAN <M> Overlay networks; needs a UDP tunnel port GENEVE <M> The newer overlay encapsulation NET_IPIP <M> Simple IPv4-in-IPv4 NET_IPGRE <M> GRE, including the keyed form IPV6_SIT <M> IPv6 in IPv4, legacy but still used XFRM_USER , INET_ESP <M> IPsec; the user interface plus the ESP transform INET_AH <M> Authentication header, rarely the right choice today Tunnels are the classic "loads on demand" case: the interface type is requested by name from userspace, and the kernel autoloads the module. If autoloading is disabled, the module has to be in the image or loaded explicitly at boot. 08 Traffic control and eBPF CONFIG_NET_SCHED=y CONFIG_NET_SCH_HTB=m CONFIG_NET_SCH_CAKE=m CONFIG_NET_SCH_FQ_CODEL=m CONFIG_NET_SCH_INGRESS=m # the hook for clsact CONFIG_NET_CLS_ACT=y # [*] actions are not optional once you classify CONFIG_NET_ACT_MIRRED=m # redirect: ingress shaping, mirroring CONFIG_NET_CLS_FLOWER=m # hardware-offloadable matching CONFIG_NET_CLS_U32=m CONFIG_NET_CLS_BPF=m CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL=y # [*] required by every eBPF tool CONFIG_BPF_JIT=y CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF=y # [*] libbpf CO-RE needs this NET_SCHED and BPF_SYSCALL are booleans; the qdiscs and classifiers are modules. A "qdisc not found" error is a missing sch_*.ko , while "Operation not supported" on a flower filter is a missing cls_flower.ko — two different messages, two different symbols. XDP is a driver property, not just a config option eBPF itself is in the core, but XDP offload needs driver support and, for the native path, a driver that implements it. On veth and tun you get the generic path; on a card that does not support it, the program simply will not attach natively. 09 Sockets that let you see Symbol Recommended Tool that breaks without it PACKET <M> tcpdump , Snort afpacket, Suricata INET_DIAG <M> ss , socket listings in monitoring agents INET_TCP_DIAG , INET_UDP_DIAG <M> Per-protocol detail for ss -t / -u UNIX_DIAG <M> ss -x NETLINK_DIAG <M> Netlink socket inspection IKCONFIG + IKCONFIG_PROC [*] /proc/config.gz — without it, no way to audit the build IKCONFIG is the cheapest hardening decision on this page: it embeds the config so anyone can check what was built, including you, two years later. Hide it if the config itself is sensitive; keep it if you would rather be auditable. 10 Options that harden by removing CONFIG_MODULE_SIG=y CONFIG_MODULE_SIG_FORCE=y # refuse unsigned modules entirely CONFIG_MODULE_UNLOAD=n # nothing can be unloaded CONFIG_KEXEC=n CONFIG_STRICT_KERNEL_RWX=y CONFIG_DEBUG_WX=y # runtime, after everything is loaded sysctl -w kernel.modules_disabled=1 MODULE_SIG_FORCE makes every module signed and trusted; a third-party driver you built yourself needs a key in the kernel keyring. MODULE_UNLOAD=n removes the ability to replace a loaded module — and the ability to recover from a bad one without rebooting. modules_disabled=1 is the strongest and least reversible: after it, no module loads. Everything the machine will ever need must already be loaded or built in. Do the arithmetic before the reboot A router that disables modules at boot must have bridging, VLAN, conntrack and the firewall built in — and the tests on this page run before the setting is permanent. The usual outcome of doing it in the other order is a machine that powers on and never passes a packet again. 11 Three role fragments These are starting points for make olddefconfig , not gospel: symbol names and defaults move between versions, and your hardware decides the driver lines. # A. Router / firewall (Debian, netfilter as modules) CONFIG_NET=y CONFIG_INET=y CONFIG_IP_ADVANCED_ROUTER=y CONFIG_IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES=y CONFIG_IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH=y CONFIG_NETFILTER=y CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK=m CONFIG_NF_NAT=m CONFIG_NF_TABLES=m CONFIG_NETFILTER_XTABLES=m CONFIG_BRIDGE=m CONFIG_VLAN_8021Q=m # B. kingdomOfTUIs: Terminal Handbook · Application Atlas Kingdom of TUIs A terminal user interface is a program that owns the screen of your terminal and behaves like an application: a file manager with panels, a monitor with graphs, a Git client with staging, a database browser. This page is a field guide to the applications you can actually install on Linux today, with their GitHub projects, so you can jump straight to the source and the README. Everything below runs inside a plain terminal on Linux. Most are single binaries or small packages; a few need a helper service (music players that speak MPD, for example). knowledgeLabyrinth: Mind · Machine · Archive God(道) Descent Knowledge Labyrinth labyrinthus Not a maze to get lost in — a descent with the lights on. Twelve layers, from the instrument in your hand to the exit condition, every wall labelled and every claim carrying a receipt. MindOS, permission lattices, kernel diffs, regression, provenance — and the psychology of anyone, this author included, who mistakes a map for the ground. OdicforceSounds Monkey Blog Technical Edition Mixed With Reality Mind · Machine · Archive — always layered Layer 0 Threshold The Entry Is Already a Model Before the first wall, the instrument. Before you enter the labyrinth, notice the instrument you are using to enter it. A browser, a reader, a terminal, a mind — each is a model of the world with its own permission lattice, its own defaults, its own hidden assumptions about what can be seen and what can be done. The labyrinth does not begin where the first wall appears. It begins where the first model is applied. That is why the first layer is always the hardest to see: you are using it to look at everything else. ⌘ Model First ◈ See the Lens ◉ Reality Has Layers "A map is not the territory, but a bad map will make you walk off the edge and call it progress." Layer 1 Map Two Maps: Territory and Procedure The labyrinth is a place and a method. There are at least two things a labyrinth can mean. One is a territory : a space of possible states, paths, dead ends, and re-entries. Knowledge, risk, identity, law, power, code — each can be drawn as a topology and then walked. The other is a procedure : a set of moves, checks, proofs, tests, audits, decisions. The labyrinth here is not a place you are lost in; it is a sequence of constraints you satisfy or fail. Both maps are real. The error is to confuse which one you are holding. Confusion What it looks like Territory mistaken for procedure You think you are walking a real space, but you are only following rules that may not fit the ground. Procedure mistaken for territory You think you are obeying a method, but you are actually wandering without one and calling it exploration. Science without procedure You claim a fact while ignoring measurement, sampling, and falsifiability. Psychology without territory You name a feeling without checking what in the world actually triggers it. "The Monkey does not choose one map. The Monkey keeps both visible and switches deliberately." Layer 2 Kinds of Real What Kind of "Real" Are We Talking About? Not one stamp. Several lenses. "Real" is not a single stamp you can put on a thing and be done. There are at least these kinds, and they behave differently under pressure: Layer What it means Tag Nominal A thing with a name and a contract around the name. Label Observed A thing inferred from repeatable measurements. Science Regulatory A thing defined by rules, jurisdiction, and enforcement. Law Structural A thing whose role is defined by how it connects, not by what it is called. Graph Operational A thing that behaves a certain way when pressure is applied. Stress Provenancial A thing whose reality is tied to its line of descent, edits, receipts, and witnesses. Trace Psychological A thing real to the organism because it shapes perception, memory, fear, and action. Mind A labyrinth made of only one kind of "real" is usually a trap dressed as depth. The Monkey prefers multi-layered: name, measurement, rule, structure, behavior, provenance, and the felt reality of a nervous system — and a clear label on which layer you are currently debating. Layer 3 MindOS Architecture of a Mind-OS A working hypothesis with visible parts. A "MindOS" is a name for a working hypothesis: an internal system that coordinates perception, memory, action, inhibition, and revision. It is not necessarily a thing you can point to and hold; it is a thing you can point to by its effects and constraints. Useful descriptions of such a system usually include, at minimum: ◈ Input Filters ◉ State ⚙ Action Selection ⊡ Inhibition ↻ Revision ⌛ Provenance MindOS — working schema Input filters what gets admitted, ignored, or flagged for later State representation what is active, dormant, or evicted right now Action selection how one candidate behavior is chosen over another Inhibition what is suppressed, and by what authority Revision when and how the system updates its own model Provenance and memory what is kept, for how long, and in what form The interesting failures are rarely "the system is not smart enough." They are usually more specific: the filters were too narrow, the state was wrong, the inhibition was too strong or too weak, the revision was too late, or the provenance was missing when it mattered. "An operating system is not wise. It is consistent under pressure — or it is not." Layer 4 Activation Activation Maps Where activity concentrates, and why. If you look at a maze from enough distance, you do not see walls first. You see flow . In a nervous system, in a network, in a body of documents, in a political field, in a person's habits — there are regions where activity clusters, and regions where it is suppressed. Call them activation maps if you want a name. The name matters less than the observability. Activation maps are interesting because they reveal structure without needing a grand theory to explain it first: Where does attention repeatedly return? Where does it fail to return even when it should? Where does activity move quickly, and where does it stall? What suppresses it — internal rules, external force, fatigue, fear, design, reward? Do not confuse "active" with "true" and do not confuse "quiet" with "unimportant." Silence can be a dead end, but it can also be a bottleneck, a concealment, or a place where the wrong thing was removed from the map on purpose. "A quiet region is not always empty. Sometimes it is policed." Layer 5 Permissions Permissions and Borders A lattice, not a wall. Borders are often drawn as lines. A better model is a lattice: many points, many relations, and many possible paths between them, some allowed, some denied, some conditional. In a system with any seriousness, permissions are not one gate. They are a lattice of decisions: R Read W Write X Execute D Delegate N Deny A Audit V Revoke Permission If missing, what breaks Read You can act without seeing what you are acting on. Write The system can be steered by whoever can alter state. Execute Intent can remain inert if it cannot be run. Delegate Authority cannot scale without it, and bottlenecks grow. Deny Without explicit denial, exception becomes the rule. Audit Without audit, permission is only a claim. Revoke Without revocation, a lost edge can stay live for too long. "A wall is what you see. A lattice is what you must walk." Layer 6 BSD Lattice On the BSD Permission Lattice A small lattice, seriously studied. Unix file modes are a small but instructive example. They are not "ownership" in any grand sense; they are a lattice of execute, write, and read rights across three classes of actor — owner, group, other — plus a few metadata flags that change how the lattice behaves in practice. The form is compact. The lessons are not: Read, write, execute are not interchangeable abstractions. Each changes the character of access in a different way. Owner/group/other are a coarse social boundary. Coarse boundaries are cheap to think about and expensive to rely on when the world is finer than the model. Setuid/setgid/sticky are not decoration. They change the effective lattice by introducing transitions and constraints that can invert who is really in control at runtime. A permission model that is "mostly right" can still be attacked through the few places where the lattice is under-specified. Study it as a toy model of a deeper problem: access is not a single bit. It is a structure of transitions, and transitions are where surprises live. Permission lattice — coarse example Class r w x real meaning Owner read write exec the named owner Group read write exec membership edge Other read write exec everyone else Layer 7 Audit Audit and the Kernel Diff What can be checked when pressure is applied. A labyrinth is not just a structure. It is a structure plus the ability to detect when it has been altered. That is the role of audit. Without audit, "permission" is a claim. With audit, it becomes a traceable decision, or at least an attempt at one. A kernel diff is one kind of trace: a record that something changed, where, and under which conditions of authority. The hard part is not producing a diff. The hard part is making the diff meaningful when the thing being changed is itself the authority that decides what counts as a valid diff. That is why serious systems think in layers again: what changed who was able to change it what that change enables next who can see the change happened who can challenge it what can revert it what can prove it was or was not reverted If any one of those is missing, the labyrinth has a blind corridor. "A change with no receipt is a claim with no spine." Layer 8 Regression Regression and Provenance The maze must be able to remember. A labyrinth that cannot say what it was yesterday is not a labyrinth worth trusting. Regression is the warning that a later state may be worse in a way that is not obvious from the immediate change. Provenance is the record that lets you ask where a state came from, which choices led to it, and which constraints were in force at the time. These two ideas belong together because they fight different failures: Concern Question it asks Tag Regression did we lose something we previously had, even if the new thing looks better on one axis? Test Provenance can we reconstruct the path that led here, and does that record survive the next change? Receipt Psychological regression does the organism revert under stress to an older, narrower response? Stress Scientific regression does the later result still survive in a broader sample or a harder test? Replicate Without regression awareness, progress becomes a one-way ratchet that may be driving you into a corner. Without provenance, responsibility becomes a fog and accountability becomes a performance. Layer 9 Descent How Descent Actually Works Go down by choice, not by accident. A labyrinth can feel like descent if you wander into it. That is the cheap version. The technical version is different: descent is deliberate, and it is tracked. Real descent has properties: You know what layer you are on, at least approximately. You know what you are giving up to go deeper. You know what would count as coming back up. You leave a trace that is readable by the standards of the layer you left, not the layer you entered. You do not confuse depth with truth, nor novelty with insight. This is where the Monkey differs from the brute. The brute wants the deep thing because it is deep. The Monkey wants the deep thing because it is auditable , repeatable , and capable of failing in a way that teaches something . ↓ Deliberate ⌛ Tracked ↩ Reversible ◉ Real Layer 10 Exit The Exit Condition Exit is also a map. If you only think about entering, you will eventually be surprised by the exit problem: what does it mean to leave this labyrinth with something real? A good exit is not "I got out." A good exit is "I can show what I carried, what I changed, what I could not verify, and where the next blind corridor is." That is the difference between exploration and tourism. Tourism wants the story of having been there. Exploration wants the map, the receipt, and the next question. "If you descend without a trace, you did not descend. You disappeared." Layer 11 Monkey The Monkey's Way Hold the opposites, keep the trace. The Monkey does not prefer the territory to the procedure, or the procedure to the territory. The Monkey prefers to be able to name which one is being used at each step. That is the deeper technical discipline here: not "more depth," but better labelling of depth . MindOS, activation maps, permission lattice, audit, kernel diff, regression, provenance — these are not decorations. They are the tools that keep descent from becoming mystification. If you want the labyrinth to be real, do not make it prettier. Make it more checkable. Make it easier to enter and leave with something you can stand behind. Make it possible to tell, after the fact, whether the walls moved or only the walker did. That is the Monkey's technical ethic. Not clean. Not simple. But traceable. ◈ Checkable ◉ Mixed ⚙ Operational ⌛ Provenanced Traceable Descent Keep the Map, Keep the Receipt Descent is not a trick. It is a discipline: model, observe, constrain, audit, remember. If you lose the map, you are not exploring. If you lose the receipt, you are not learning. If you lose both, you are just moving. ← Back Top The Monkey O Macaco Path & Dream

learnHacking: How Hacking Happens — And How To Stop It Blue team to understand attack paths. Red team to break them. Lab only. No real targets without written permission. Ever. Ethics first — read or close this file: Only hack systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test (your lab, CTF, bug-bounty scope). Unauthorized access, credential cracking against real accounts, malware, ransomware, doxxing = crimes. This manual teaches concepts + defense + lab practice , not how to break into real systems. If in doubt, defend. 0 — Map: Hats, Teams, Bounties White hat: authorized defender/researcher. Black hat: criminal. Gray hat: unauthorized but claims good intent — still illegal, don't. Red team: authorized adversary emulation. Blue team: detect/respond/harden. Purple: both collaborate. Bug bounty: legal hacking inside a scope + rules (see HackerOne , Bugcrowd , GitHub Security Lab ). Start with OWASP Top 10 + OWASP Testing Guide . Papers to read (defensive lens): NIST SP 800 series (800-53, 800-115 testing) , MITRE ATT&CK (adversary tactics map), Cyber Kill Chain (Lockheed), NIST Incident Handling 800-61 . 1 — Lab, Not Real Life: Isolate Your Experiments Build a lab you can break without breaking law or others: Host: Debian/Ubuntu, updated, firewall on Hypervisor: VirtualBox (https://www.virtualbox.org/) or KVM/QEMU + virt-manager Net: Host-only / NAT, NO bridge to home LAN for vulnerable VMs Targets (vulnerable-by-design, local only): - Metasploitable 2/3 (https://github.com/rapid7/metasploitable3) - OWASP Juice Shop (https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop) - DVWA (https://github.com/digininja/DVWA) - WebGoat (https://github.com/WebGoat/WebGoat) Attacker: Kali Linux (https://www.kali.org/) as a toolbox, snapshots before/after Capture: Wireshark (https://www.wireshark.org/) on host-only only Snapshot everything. Lab firewall: vulnerable VMs must never reach internet. No real credentials, no real data, no scanning outside 192.168.56.0/24 lab range. Secure your lab: separate user, encrypted disk ( LUKS docs ), ufw deny incoming on host, VPN kill-switch if you must fetch tools, GPG-verify ISOs. 2 — How Attacks Are Structured (Kill Chain → ATT&CK, Defensive View) Recon → weaponize → deliver → exploit → install → command → act. Map each to ATT&CK tactics. Blue counters: harden, detect, segment, log, respond. Example: phishing (Initial Access) fails if MFA + user training + mail filtering win. Study NIST CSF : Govern/Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond/Recover. 3 — Recon & Scanning: What Attackers See, How Defenders Shrink It Concept: DNS, subdomains, ports, services, versions leak attack surface. Tools defenders use to audit own scope: Nmap ( nmap.org , github/nmap ), Amass ( owasp-amass ), theHarvester ( theHarvester ), Shodan ( shodan.io — defender search for own exposure). # LAB ONLY against your own VMs, e.g. 192.168.56.101: nmap -sV -O 192.168.56.101 # versions, OS guess — then YOU patch/hide them # Blue: close ports, least service, banner minimization, WAF/CDN in front Blue lesson: every open port/version you see, attacker sees. Inventory with Nmap , then firewall, update, segment. Log scans with Suricata / Snort . 4 — Web: The #1 Real-World Path (Understand → Fix) Learn OWASP Top 10 : injection, broken access control, XSS, SSRF, misconfig. Practice defensively on Juice Shop / DVWA locally; intercept with Burp Suite Community ( portswigger ) or OWASP ZAP ( zaproxy , github ). Defense pattern (the point): parameterize queries, ORM, allow-list validation ( Zod ), output-encode, CSP + HttpOnly/SameSite cookies via Helmet ( helmetjs ), strict access checks server-side, SSRF allow-lists + no cloud metadata access. Scan own code with Semgrep , deps with Grype . 5 — C Fundamentals: Stack, Memory, Why Safe Code Matters You don't need to exploit to defend — but you must grasp why memory bugs are critical. Theory only, lab only: // stack frame (simplified x86-64): high -> low // [args][ret addr][saved rbp][locals: char buf[64]] // Unsafe copy can overflow locals -> crash/hijack in theory. // Defense: -fstack-protector-strong -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -Wl,-z,RelRO,-z,Now -fPIE -pie // + ASLR, NX, canaries, fuzzing, modern langs (Rust/Go) for new code. Learn safely: RPISEC MBE (course), pwn.college (ASU, lab + defense), awesome-pwn (curated learning) , papers: Smashing the Stack (Phrack 49, historic) — read as history + why mitigations exist. Practice defense: compile with protections, run ASan/UBSan , fuzz with AFL++ on your own code, verify with checksec / hardening-check . 6 — Passwords/Cracking: Why We Harden Auth (No Real Cracking) Concept: weak/reused passwords + no MFA = breach. Attackers use leaked lists + guessing in theory; your job is to make it fail : long unique passwords in KeePassXC ( keepassxc.org ), MFA everywhere (TOTP/WebAuthn), bcrypt/argon2 server-side, rate-limit + lockout, breach monitoring ( HIBP ). Audit own hashes in lab only with John ( openwall ) / Hashcat ( hashcat ) docs to prove policy works — never against others. 7 — Blue Team: Detect, Log, Respond Tools: Wireshark ( wireshark ) for packets, Suricata / Snort IDS, Wazuh ( wazuh , github ) SIEM, TheHive+Cortex ( TheHive ) case mgmt, Velociraptor ( velociraptor ) DFIR, Ghidra ( ghidra , NSA github ) for malware analysis in isolated VM . Playbooks: NIST 800-61 , SANS whitepapers . Log centrally, time-sync (NTP), alert on ATT&CK techniques you actually see in lab, rehearse restore from offline backups. Blue wins by preparation, not heroics. 8 — Bug Bounty Path (Legal Hacking Career) 1) Learn web + networking basics. 2) Lab: Juice Shop → PortSwigger Academy ( portswigger academy ). 3) Read scopes twice, respect out-of-scope, rate limits, disclosure rules. 4) Report: repro, impact, fix. Repos: OWASP WSTG checklist , HackTricks (defensive reference — use on own scope only) , PayloadsAllTheThings (test payloads for own lab/scope) . Never extort, never pivot beyond scope, never access real user data. 9 — Study Plan (6 Weeks, Lab + Defense) W1 Linux+networking + lab build. W2 OWASP Top 10 on Juice Shop + fix code. W3 Nmap/ZAP on own VMs + harden. W4 C/memory theory + compiler mitigations + fuzz own toy program. W5 Blue: Suricata+Wazuh alerts + IR drill. W6 Bounty-style report on lab target with fix PR. Throughout: ATT&CK mapping, write-ups, clean snapshots. Hack to protect. Learn stacks to build safer stacks. The best hacker on your network is the defender you trained.
